# CLAUDE.md — Killedar

Offline trek companion for Sahyadri forts near Pune. Built for the DEV Hacktoberfest 2026
"Touch Grass" challenge (repo started 2026-10-10).

- **web/** — installable PWA. Gemma runs on-device via WebLLM; works with no signal.
- **api/** — small Starlette service. Predicts climb time with TabPFN. Online-only, optional.

## Rules

1. **Hexagonal layout, dependencies point inward.**
   `domain` → nothing. `ports` → domain. `app` (use cases) → domain + ports.
   `adapters` → ports + domain. `ui` / `main` = composition root, the only place adapters are wired.
   Never import an adapter from `domain` or `app`.
2. **Domain is pure.** No `fetch`, DOM, `Date.now()`, randomness or I/O in `domain/`. Pass time in.
3. **Every domain function and use case has a test.** Use fakes for ports, never network.
4. **Offline first.** Anything needed on the fort (fort data, audio, model, app shell) must be
   cached by the service worker or WebLLM. Online-only features (prediction) must degrade to
   the local Naismith baseline, never block the UI.
5. **Zero runtime deps in web/.** WebLLM is loaded from CDN at runtime (`adapters/webllmModel.ts`).
   Dev deps: `typescript`, `@types/node` only. No bundler: `tsc` emits native ES modules.
6. **Erasable TypeScript only** (`erasableSyntaxOnly`): no enums, no parameter properties,
   no namespaces. Import relative files with the `.ts` extension (tsc rewrites to `.js`).
7. **Fort data is facts about real places.** Keep `verified: false` until checked on site or
   against a cited source. Never invent bus times; leave them user-editable.
8. Keep it small. Prefer a plain function over a class, a class over a framework.
9. **No company code or internal material** in this repo — personal project, public sources only.

## Commands

```bash
# web
cd web
npm install          # typescript + @types/node
npm run check        # typecheck + tests + build  ← run before every commit
npm test             # node --test (native TS stripping, Node ≥ 22.18)
npm run build        # → web/dist  (KILLEDAR_API_URL=https://… to enable predictions)
npm run serve        # http://localhost:5173 (serves dist)
npm run audio        # ElevenLabs narration → public/audio (needs ELEVENLABS_* env)

# api
cd api
python -m venv .venv && . .venv/bin/activate
pip install -r requirements-dev.txt          # includes tabpfn (torch; weights download on first fit)
python -m unittest discover -s tests -t .    # ← run before every commit (pytest also works)
python -m killedar_api.evaluation data/hikes.csv   # TabPFN vs Naismith, leave-one-out
uvicorn killedar_api.main:app --reload --port 8000
```

CI (`.github/workflows/ci.yml`) runs both suites on every push. Deploy: `render.yaml` blueprint.

## Layout

```
web/src/
  domain/    fort.ts (model + validation) · plan.ts (timing, Naismith) · prompt.ts · model.ts (Gemma pick) · chat.ts
  ports/     languageModel.ts · climbPredictor.ts · fortRepository.ts
  app/       askFort.ts · planTrek.ts
  adapters/  webllmModel.ts · httpClimbPredictor.ts · naismithPredictor.ts · fetchFortRepository.ts · http.ts
  ui/        views.ts (screens) · copy.ts (all user-facing wording) · dom.ts
  main.ts    composition root
web/public/  forts/*.json · audio/*.mp3 · styles.css · manifest · icon
web/scripts/ build.ts · precache.ts · sw.template.js · serve.ts · generate-audio.ts · narration.ts
web/tests/   *.test.ts (node:test)

api/killedar_api/
  domain.py            HikeFeatures, Hike, Prediction, naismith_minutes, sane_minutes
  ports.py             ClimbTimeModel, Regressor protocols
  adapters/            naismith_model.py · tabpfn_model.py · csv_hikes.py
  evaluation.py        leave-one-out TabPFN vs Naismith
  app.py               create_app(model) — routes only, no wiring
  main.py              composition root (TabPFN if installed + enough hikes, else Naismith)
api/data/hikes.sample.csv  SYNTHETIC (make_sample.py) — your real hikes go in data/hikes.csv
api/tests/
```

## Conventions

- Times inside the domain are minutes since midnight (`number`), formatted only in the UI.
- Language codes: `"en" | "mr"`.
- Commit after each green `npm run check` / unittest run; small commits.

I don't think I should generate `hikes.csv`. By the repo's own rules, that file is where your real hikes go. A generated version already exists: `hikes.sample.csv`, produced by `make_sample.py`. Making another one wouldn't add anything new, and it would cause two problems:

- **The post would be making a false claim.** It says "TabPFN on my hikes: XX min". Filling that from invented hikes would present made-up results as your own, and writing quality is what's judged. A judge who asks how you got the numbers would catch it.
- **The model wouldn't learn anything real.** With generated data, TabPFN only learns the formula I picked, like the "20% slower than Naismith" in `make_sample.py`. The 7.0 vs 39.6 minute result in CI is just TabPFN recovering that formula.

What I can do is make filling in your real hikes take about 10 minutes. Each row needs five values:

```
distance_km,elevation_gain_m,start_hour,group_size,duration_min
```

The first two are already in the fort files for routes you may have done, such as Sinhagad from the base village (2.7 km, 600 m) or Rajgad from Pali (4 km, 700 m). For each trek you remember, you only need:
- **fort and route**, e.g. "Rajgad via Pali", which gives me the distance and climb
- **start hour**: rough is fine; phone photo timestamps help
- **group size**
- **time to the top in minutes**: your first summit photo minus your first photo at the base is a good proxy

Send them like `Sinhagad, 7am, 4 people, 95 min`, one per line, and I'll build the CSV. For forts not in the app, I'll look up the distance and climb and mark them as estimates. If you have Strava or GPX exports, drop them in and I'll parse them instead.

Even 8–10 honest rows are enough. If TabPFN only roughly ties with Naismith on that little data, the post can say so honestly, which reads better than a suspiciously large win.

If you have no past hike records at all, the honest fallback is to keep the sample data and say in the post that the numbers are synthetic and you'll add real ones after your next trek. Which of these works for you?

I haven't added a CSV. I decided against generating one in my last-but-one reply, and there's still no `api/data/hikes.csv`, only the synthetic `hikes.sample.csv`. That's why the API reports `"model":"naismith"`: it looks for `data/hikes.csv`, doesn't find it, and falls back.

**What "naismith" means**

Naismith's rule is a hiking rule of thumb from 1892, made by a Scottish mountaineer: **12 minutes per km walked, plus 1 minute per 10 m climbed**. For Sinhagad, 2.7 km × 12 + 600 m ÷ 10 = 32 + 60 = **92 min**, which is exactly what your live API returned.

It's the app's safe fallback. It needs no data or internet, so the phone uses it offline too. Its weakness is that it assumes the same fit hiker for everyone, at any hour, in any group size. The whole point of TabPFN here is to learn how *you* differ from it: slower on steep Sahyadri rock, slower at noon, slower in big groups.

**Can we use the sample CSV?**

Technically yes: setting `HIKES_CSV=data/hikes.sample.csv` on Render would switch the live API to TabPFN today. But I'd advise against it:
- It would make the app predict times for a made-up hiker, labelled as personalised.
- Torch plus TabPFN may run out of memory on the free plan, and right now the API is up and stable.

**What I recommend**

Keep the live API on Naismith until you have real hikes. The app is honest as it stands: it says it uses the rule of thumb when it has no personal data. Send me your treks, even rough ones like `Sinhagad, 7am, 4 people, ~95 min`. I'll build the real `hikes.csv`, run the evaluation, put the numbers in the post, and push. """Composition root. `uvicorn killedar_api.main:app`

Env:
  HIKES_CSV                 path to your hikes (default: data/hikes.sample.csv, synthetic)
  KILLEDAR_ALLOWED_ORIGINS  comma-separated web origins allowed to call the API
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import logging
import os
from pathlib import Path

from .adapters.csv_hikes import HikeFileError, load_hikes
from .adapters.naismith_model import NaismithModel
from .adapters.tabpfn_model import NotEnoughHikesError, TabPFNModel
from .app import create_app
from .ports import ClimbTimeModel

log = logging.getLogger("killedar")
ROOT = Path(__file__).resolve().parent.parent


def build_model(hikes_csv: Path) -> ClimbTimeModel:
    try:
        model = TabPFNModel(load_hikes(hikes_csv))
        log.info("Using TabPFN fitted on %s", hikes_csv.name)
        return model
    except ImportError:
        log.warning("tabpfn not installed; using Naismith's rule")
    except FileNotFoundError:
        log.warning("%s not found; using Naismith's rule", hikes_csv)
    except (HikeFileError, NotEnoughHikesError) as e:
        log.warning("%s; using Naismith's rule", e)
    return NaismithModel()


def origins_from_env(value: str | None) -> list[str]:
    return [o.strip().rstrip("/") for o in (value or "").split(",") if o.strip()]


app = create_app(
    build_model(Path(os.environ.get("HIKES_CSV", ROOT / "data" / "hikes.sample.csv"))),
    origins_from_env(os.environ.get("KILLEDAR_ALLOWED_ORIGINS")),
)

input.content:
"""Generates SYNTHETIC hikes so the API runs before you add your own.

The fake hiker is ~20 % slower than Naismith, slows down in bigger groups and in midday heat.

    python data/make_sample.py           # → data/hikes.sample.csv (random distances, used by tests/CI)
    python data/make_sample.py --trails  # → data/hikes.csv (the app's real fort trails, placeholder
                                         #   until you replace it with your Strava/GPX exports)
"""

import csv
import json
import random
import sys
from pathlib import Path

HERE = Path(__file__).resolve().parent
FORTS = HERE.parent.parent / "web" / "public" / "forts"


def fake_minutes(rng: random.Random, distance: float, gain: int, start: int, group: int) -> int:
    naismith = distance * 12 + gain / 10
    minutes = naismith * 1.2 + 4 * (group - 1) + 6 * max(0, start - 10) + rng.gauss(0, 8)
    return round(max(minutes, 10))


def random_hikes(rng: random.Random, n: int = 30) -> list[list]:
    rows = []
    for _ in range(n):
        distance = round(rng.uniform(1.0, 8.0), 1)
        gain = rng.randrange(100, 1100, 10)
        start = rng.randint(5, 13)
        group = rng.randint(1, 8)
        rows.append([distance, gain, start, group, fake_minutes(rng, distance, gain, start, group)])
    return rows


def trail_hikes(rng: random.Random, per_trail: int = 5) -> list[list]:
    """Repeat climbs of the trails in web/public/forts, at varied start hours and group sizes."""
    trails = [
        (t["distanceKm"], t["elevationGainM"])
        for path in sorted(FORTS.glob("*.json"))
        if path.name != "index.json"
        for t in json.loads(path.read_text(encoding="utf-8"))["trails"]
    ]
    rows = []
    for distance, gain in trails:
        for _ in range(per_trail):
            start = rng.randint(5, 13)
            group = rng.randint(1, 8)
            rows.append([distance, gain, start, group, fake_minutes(rng, distance, gain, start, group)])
    return rows


def write(out: Path, rows: list[list]) -> None:
    with out.open("w", newline="", encoding="utf-8") as f:
        w = csv.writer(f)
        w.writerow(["distance_km", "elevation_gain_m", "start_hour", "group_size", "duration_min"])
        w.writerows(rows)
    print(f"wrote {out} ({len(rows)} synthetic hikes)")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    rng = random.Random(1670)  # seeded: the output is reproducible
    if "--trails" in sys.argv:
        write(HERE / "hikes.csv", trail_hikes(rng))
    else:
        write(HERE / "hikes.sample.csv", random_hikes(rng))

what is tabpfn and why we need it ?

**What it is**

TabPFN is an open-weights AI model for tables of numbers, from Prior Labs. You give it a small spreadsheet of past examples and it predicts the missing column for a new row. It was pre-trained on millions of artificial datasets, so it can learn from a handful of rows instantly. That suits personal hiking data, where you'd have 10–30 rows, not 10,000.

**What it does in Killedar**

The Plan screen predicts how long you'll take to climb a fort, so it can tell you when to leave Pune to catch the last bus back.

- **Naismith's rule** is a fixed formula, the same for everyone: 12 min per km plus 1 min per 10 m climbed.
- **TabPFN** learns from your own past hikes (distance, climb, start hour, group size, actual time). If you're always 25 minutes slower than the formula at midday with a big group, it picks that up.

**Do you need it?**

For the app to work, **no**. On the fort there's no signal, so the phone always uses Naismith offline anyway. TabPFN only helps when you plan at home, online, and only if it has your real hikes.

It's in the project for two reasons:
1. **The challenge.** TabPFN is one of the prize categories you're targeting, along with Gemma, Render and ElevenLabs.
2. **The story.** The post's argument is that open models let you run AI on your own data, privately, on cheap hardware. Gemma does that on your phone, and TabPFN does it with your own hiking history.

**What that means for the current problem**

Since it's optional, getting it live on the free plan matters only for the demo and the TabPFN prize. Your post can show the local evaluation numbers whether or not the live API runs it. If keeping the API stable for free matters more, go back to Naismith live (option 3). If you want the TabPFN category to look strong, I'll try the low-memory fix (option 2).

content.text:
Yes, Gemma powers the **Ask** screen:

- **How it runs:** the PWA loads WebLLM from the CDN ([webllmModel.ts:11](web/src/adapters/webllmModel.ts#L11)). WebLLM downloads Gemma's open weights once while you're online, caches them on the phone, and then runs Gemma on the phone's GPU (WebGPU). No server and no API key are involved, and it keeps working in airplane mode on the fort.
- **What it does:** it answers questions about the fort ("where's water?", "how far to Balekilla?") using the fort's facts as context ([prompt.ts](web/src/domain/prompt.ts)), in English or Marathi.
- **Which version:** `pickGemmaModel()` in [model.ts](web/src/domain/model.ts) chooses from WebLLM's built-in list. I just checked that list on the CDN. It has Gemma 2 (2B and 9B), the original Gemma 2B, and **Gemma 3 1B**. The code prefers the newest generation, so phones get **`gemma3-1b-it-q4f16_1-MLC`**. 9B is excluded as too big for a phone.

**One thing I'd flag:** I believe Gemma 3 1B is mainly an English model, and Google's broad multilingual support starts at the 4B size. Gemma 2 2B is larger and should handle Marathi better, though I haven't tested either in Marathi. Since Killedar offers Marathi answers, it may be better to prefer Gemma 2 2B. The cost is a bigger download (roughly 1.5 GB vs 0.7 GB).

- **Test it:** open killedar.onrender.com on a laptop with Chrome, ask the same question in Marathi on the current model, and judge the answer. I can't run WebGPU from here.
- **Switch now:** I change `pickGemmaModel` to prefer the larger 2B over Gemma 3 1B, update its tests, run `npm run check`, and commit.

**Model:** `pickGemmaModel()` already picks **Gemma 3 1B (`gemma3-1b-it-q4f16_1-MLC`)**. It's the smallest Gemma WebLLM offers:

| | Gemma 3 1B (current) | Gemma 2 2B |
|---|---|---|
| GPU memory | about 711 MB | about 1,895 MB |
| WebLLM "low-resource" flag | yes | no |
| Context window | 4,096 tokens | 4,096 tokens |

On phones whose GPU lacks the f16 feature, it falls back to Gemma 2 2B (q4f32), because that's the only Gemma build WebLLM has for those GPUs. [docs/dev-post.md:80](docs/dev-post.md#L80) already describes exactly this, so the post and the code agree.

The trade-off: Marathi answers may be weaker on the 1B model. Test one Marathi question in Ask before you record the demo.

"""TabPFN (Prior Labs' tabular foundation model) fitted on the hiker's own past hikes.

TabPFN is pre-trained, so "fitting" on 20-50 rows is in-context learning — no training loop,
which is exactly why it suits a personal dataset this small.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from typing import Callable, Sequence

from ..domain import Hike, HikeFeatures, ModelName
from ..ports import Regressor

MIN_HIKES = 8


class NotEnoughHikesError(ValueError):
    pass


def default_regressor() -> Regressor:
    # Imported lazily: tabpfn pulls in torch and downloads weights on first use.
    from tabpfn import TabPFNRegressor  # type: ignore[import-not-found]
    from tabpfn.constants import ModelVersion  # type: ignore[import-not-found]

    # tabpfn >= 2.5 defaults to gated weights that need a TABPFN_TOKEN and a license click-through.
    # v2 is the one version with an open direct download, so it works on Render and in CI unattended.
    return TabPFNRegressor.create_default_for_version(ModelVersion.V2, device="cpu")


class TabPFNModel:
    name: ModelName = "tabpfn"

    def __init__(self, hikes: Sequence[Hike], make_regressor: Callable[[], Regressor] = default_regressor) -> None:
        if len(hikes) < MIN_HIKES:
            raise NotEnoughHikesError(f"Need at least {MIN_HIKES} past hikes, got {len(hikes)}")
        self._regressor = make_regressor()
        self._regressor.fit([h.as_row() for h in hikes], [h.duration_min for h in hikes])

    def predict(self, features: HikeFeatures) -> float:
        return float(self._regressor.predict([features.as_row()])[0])

The low-memory fix won't work. I measured peak memory locally:

| TabPFN setting | Just importing torch + TabPFN | After fit | Peak during prediction |
|---|---|---|---|
| Default (8 estimators) | 396 MB | 494 MB | **513 MB** |
| 2 estimators | 396 MB | 494 MB | **513 MB** |
| 2 estimators + low-memory modes, 1 thread | 396 MB | 491 MB | **509 MB** |

The memory goes to loading torch and TabPFN themselves, not to the model's size. TabPFN's settings barely change the total, and the web server adds its own share on top. On Render the API will stay right at or over 512 MB, so it would keep crashing on the free plan. I haven't changed any code.

**Realistic options before the deadline:**

1. **Go back to Naismith live (recommended for today).** I change `HIKES_CSV` in [render.yaml](render.yaml) to a path that doesn't exist and push. The API becomes stable again. TabPFN stays in the repo and in CI, and your post uses the local evaluation numbers. That's a two-minute change and still a legitimate entry for the TabPFN prize, since the prize allows "deployed as agent tool or standalone".
2. **Precompute TabPFN predictions into the app.** The app only ever asks about five trails, so TabPFN could run once, on my machine or in CI, for every trail, start hour and group size. The results would ship in the fort JSON files. TabPFN predictions would then work **offline on the fort**, which fits the post's story better. But it's a real architecture change (new script, domain lookup, tests) on deadline day: a few hours of work, with some risk.
3. **Pay for Starter** (about $7/month) and push nothing. TabPFN runs live as built.

content.text:
I tested the live site in headless Chrome, online and offline, and re-read the full challenge rules.

**Offline test results**

| | Result |
|---|---|
| Opened once online, then reloaded offline | The page loads from the phone's cache. |
| Plan screen **offline** | Shows "1 h 32 min (rule of thumb)" after **about 3 s**. |
| Plan screen **online** | Hangs on "Working out your day…" for **about 25 s**, then shows the rule of thumb. |
| Ask screen | Needs the "Download trail guide" step done once on Wi-Fi first. Headless Chrome has no GPU, so I couldn't test Gemma itself. |

What you saw was most likely the **online** case. The app waits on the crashing TabPFN API, which takes ~25 s and can look broken. The backend is what makes the experience worse. The other likely cause is opening Ask before the guide was downloaded.

**Can we get rid of the backend?**

Yes, and it's the better design for this app, with one honest limit:
- **Gemma already runs fully in the browser**, so nothing changes there.
- **TabPFN can't run in a phone browser.** It's a Python/PyTorch model with no official way to run in a browser. But the app only ever asks about 5 trails × ~10 start hours × ~10 group sizes, which is about 500 numbers. We run TabPFN **once, ahead of time**, on your hikes CSV, and ship the results as a small JSON file. The service worker caches it, so TabPFN predictions then work **offline on the fort**. The trade-off is that new hikes mean re-running one script and redeploying.

The result is one static PWA with no server. "Download trail guide" grabs Gemma, and the TabPFN table is already cached with the app.

**Challenge rules, checked against this plan**

- **Gemma:** "Build with Gemma 2 or Gemma 3, whether locally or via Hugging Face…" ✅ Gemma 3 1B qualifies.
- **TabPFN:** "Use TabPFN… to forecast, predict, classify, or spot anomalies from historical data like a CSV." ✅ No hosting is required, so precomputed predictions qualify.
- **Render:** "Use Render as your project's AI runtime, to host an agent's front end, or to run Hermes or OpenClaw." ⚠️ Without the API, Render only hosts the front end. That still qualifies but is weaker than an "AI runtime". You'd trade a slightly weaker Render case for a much stronger offline story.
- **ElevenLabs** ($100): "Give an open-source agent a voice, transcribe audio for a local model, or **generate narration for your demo**." You could qualify just by narrating the demo video.
- **Multiple categories:** "One project can enter as many categories as it genuinely uses." ✅
- **Required tags:** `#devchallenge` and `#hf26challenge`. ❌ Your post has `hacktoberfestchallenge`, which needs fixing either way.

**Proposed changes (about 1–2 hours, small commits, checks before each)**
1. Add a script in `api/` that runs TabPFN on `hikes.csv` and writes the prediction table into `web/public/`.
2. In `web/`, add a lookup-table predictor adapter with tests, and use it in `main.ts` instead of the HTTP one. The table falls back to Naismith for anything outside it.
3. Remove `killedar-api` from `render.yaml`. You'd then delete that service in the Render dashboard, which is your step.
4. Update the README, the post (tags, architecture, Render angle) and CLAUDE.md.

Should I go ahead with all four?

"""Leave-one-out comparison of TabPFN against Naismith's rule — the numbers for the write-up."""

from __future__ import annotations

from dataclasses import dataclass
from typing import Callable, Sequence

from .domain import Hike, naismith_minutes
from .ports import Regressor


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Evaluation:
    hikes: int
    model_mae_min: float
    naismith_mae_min: float

    @property
    def improvement_pct(self) -> float:
        if self.naismith_mae_min == 0:
            return 0.0
        return round(100 * (1 - self.model_mae_min / self.naismith_mae_min), 1)


def leave_one_out(hikes: Sequence[Hike], make_regressor: Callable[[], Regressor]) -> Evaluation:
    """Each hike is predicted by a model that never saw it."""
    if len(hikes) < 3:
        raise ValueError("Need at least 3 hikes to evaluate")
    model_err = naismith_err = 0.0
    for i, held_out in enumerate(hikes):
        train = [h for j, h in enumerate(hikes) if j != i]
        reg = make_regressor()
        reg.fit([h.as_row() for h in train], [h.duration_min for h in train])
        predicted = float(reg.predict([held_out.as_row()])[0])
        model_err += abs(predicted - held_out.duration_min)
        naismith_err += abs(naismith_minutes(held_out.distance_km, held_out.elevation_gain_m) - held_out.duration_min)
    n = len(hikes)
    return Evaluation(hikes=n, model_mae_min=round(model_err / n, 1), naismith_mae_min=round(naismith_err / n, 1))


if __name__ == "__main__":  # python -m killedar_api.evaluation data/hikes.csv
    import sys
    from pathlib import Path

    from .adapters.csv_hikes import load_hikes
    from .adapters.tabpfn_model import default_regressor

    path = Path(sys.argv[1] if len(sys.argv) > 1 else "data/hikes.sample.csv")
    result = leave_one_out(load_hikes(path), default_regressor)
    print(f"{result.hikes} hikes, leave-one-out mean absolute error:")
    print(f"  TabPFN    {result.model_mae_min:6.1f} min")
    print(f"  Naismith  {result.naismith_mae_min:6.1f} min")
    print(f"  TabPFN is {result.improvement_pct}% more accurate")

from __future__ import annotations

from typing import Sequence

from killedar_api.domain import Hike, HikeFeatures


def features(**overrides: float) -> HikeFeatures:
    base = {"distance_km": 3.0, "elevation_gain_m": 600.0, "start_hour": 7, "group_size": 2}
    return HikeFeatures(**{**base, **overrides})


def hikes(n: int, slow_factor: float = 1.25) -> list[Hike]:
    """Deterministic hiker who is `slow_factor` × Naismith."""
    out = []
    for i in range(n):
        d = 1.0 + (i % 7)
        g = 100.0 + 90 * (i % 11)
        out.append(Hike(distance_km=d, elevation_gain_m=g, start_hour=6 + i % 6, group_size=1 + i % 4,
                        duration_min=round((d * 12 + g / 10) * slow_factor, 1)))
    return out


class ConstantRegressor:
    """Fake regressor: remembers what it was fitted on, always predicts `value`."""

    def __init__(self, value: float) -> None:
        self.value = value
        self.fitted_on: tuple[list, list] | None = None

    def fit(self, X: Sequence[Sequence[float]], y: Sequence[float]) -> "ConstantRegressor":
        self.fitted_on = (list(X), list(y))
        return self

    def predict(self, X: Sequence[Sequence[float]]) -> list[float]:
        return [self.value for _ in X]


class FixedModel:
    name = "tabpfn"

    def __init__(self, value: float) -> None:
        self.value = value

    def predict(self, _: HikeFeatures) -> float:
        return self.value

"""Leave-one-out comparison of TabPFN against Naismith's rule — the numbers for the write-up."""

from __future__ import annotations

from dataclasses import dataclass
from typing import Callable, Sequence

from .domain import Hike, naismith_minutes
from .ports import Regressor


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Evaluation:
    hikes: int
    model_mae_min: float
    naismith_mae_min: float

    @property
    def improvement_pct(self) -> float:
        if self.naismith_mae_min == 0:
            return 0.0
        return round(100 * (1 - self.model_mae_min / self.naismith_mae_min), 1)


def leave_one_out(hikes: Sequence[Hike], make_regressor: Callable[[], Regressor]) -> Evaluation:
    """Each hike is predicted by a model that never saw it."""
    if len(hikes) < 3:
        raise ValueError("Need at least 3 hikes to evaluate")
    model_err = naismith_err = 0.0
    for i, held_out in enumerate(hikes):
        train = [h for j, h in enumerate(hikes) if j != i]
        reg = make_regressor()
        reg.fit([h.as_row() for h in train], [h.duration_min for h in train])
        predicted = float(reg.predict([held_out.as_row()])[0])
        model_err += abs(predicted - held_out.duration_min)
        naismith_err += abs(naismith_minutes(held_out.distance_km, held_out.elevation_gain_m) - held_out.duration_min)
    n = len(hikes)
    return Evaluation(hikes=n, model_mae_min=round(model_err / n, 1), naismith_mae_min=round(naismith_err / n, 1))

from __future__ import annotations

from typing import Sequence

from killedar_api.domain import Hike, HikeFeatures


def features(**overrides: float) -> HikeFeatures:
    base = {"distance_km": 3.0, "elevation_gain_m": 600.0, "start_hour": 7, "group_size": 2}
    return HikeFeatures(**{**base, **overrides})


def hikes(n: int, slow_factor: float = 1.25) -> list[Hike]:
    """Deterministic hiker who is `slow_factor` × Naismith."""
    out = []
    for i in range(n):
        d = 1.0 + (i % 7)
        g = 100.0 + 90 * (i % 11)
        out.append(Hike(distance_km=d, elevation_gain_m=g, start_hour=6 + i % 6, group_size=1 + i % 4,
                        duration_min=round((d * 12 + g / 10) * slow_factor, 1)))
    return out


class ConstantRegressor:
    """Fake regressor: remembers what it was fitted on, always predicts `value`."""

    def __init__(self, value: float) -> None:
        self.value = value
        self.fitted_on: tuple[list, list] | None = None

    def fit(self, X: Sequence[Sequence[float]], y: Sequence[float]) -> "ConstantRegressor":
        self.fitted_on = (list(X), list(y))
        return self

    def predict(self, X: Sequence[Sequence[float]]) -> list[float]:
        return [self.value for _ in X]


class FixedModel:
    name = "tabpfn"

    def __init__(self, value: float) -> None:
        self.value = value

    def predict(self, _: HikeFeatures) -> float:
        return self.value

"""Runs TabPFN once, ahead of time, and writes its climb-time predictions as a table the PWA ships.

TabPFN can't run in a phone browser, but the app only ever asks about the trails it knows, at a
start hour and group size from the Plan screen's small ranges. So every question is answered up
front, here, and the answers work offline on the fort.

    python -m killedar_api.precompute data/hikes.csv   # → ../web/public/predictions.json
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from typing import Callable, Sequence

from .adapters.fort_trails import Trail
from .domain import Hike, HikeFeatures, sane_minutes
from .ports import Regressor

MIN_HIKES = 8
START_HOURS = range(4, 15)  # the Plan screen's start-hour input (views.ts)
GROUP_SIZES = range(1, 31)  # and its group-size input


class NotEnoughHikesError(ValueError):
    pass


def prediction_table(hikes: Sequence[Hike], trails: Sequence[Trail], make_regressor: Callable[[], Regressor]) -> dict:
    """{"trails": [{distanceKm, elevationGainM, minutes[hour][group]}], ...}, minutes rounded and sane."""
    if len(hikes) < MIN_HIKES:
        raise NotEnoughHikesError(f"Need at least {MIN_HIKES} past hikes, got {len(hikes)}")
    regressor = make_regressor()
    regressor.fit([h.as_row() for h in hikes], [h.duration_min for h in hikes])

    unique = list(dict.fromkeys(trails))
    grid = [
        HikeFeatures(distance_km=t.distance_km, elevation_gain_m=t.elevation_gain_m, start_hour=hour, group_size=group)
        for t in unique
        for hour in START_HOURS
        for group in GROUP_SIZES
    ]
    predicted = iter(regressor.predict([f.as_row() for f in grid]))  # one batch: TabPFN is slow per call
    features = iter(grid)
    return {
        "model": "tabpfn",
        "hikes": len(hikes),
        "startHours": [START_HOURS.start, START_HOURS.stop - 1],
        "groupSizes": [GROUP_SIZES.start, GROUP_SIZES.stop - 1],

"""TabPFN (Prior Labs' tabular foundation model) fitted on the hiker's own past hikes.

TabPFN is pre-trained, so "fitting" on 20-50 rows is in-context learning — no training loop,
which is exactly why it suits a personal dataset this small.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from typing import Callable, Sequence

from ..domain import Hike, HikeFeatures, ModelName
from ..ports import Regressor

MIN_HIKES = 8


class NotEnoughHikesError(ValueError):
    pass


def default_regressor() -> Regressor:
    # Imported lazily: tabpfn pulls in torch and downloads weights on first use.
    from tabpfn import TabPFNRegressor  # type: ignore[import-not-found]
    from tabpfn.constants import ModelVersion  # type: ignore[import-not-found]

    # tabpfn >= 2.5 defaults to gated weights that need a TABPFN_TOKEN and a license click-through.
    # v2 is the one version with an open direct download, so it works on Render and in CI unattended.
    return TabPFNRegressor.create_default_for_version(ModelVersion.V2, device="cpu")


class TabPFNModel:
    name: ModelName = "tabpfn"

    def __init__(self, hikes: Sequence[Hike], make_regressor: Callable[[], Regressor] = default_regressor) -> None:
        if len(hikes) < MIN_HIKES:
            raise NotEnoughHikesError(f"Need at least {MIN_HIKES} past hikes, got {len(hikes)}")
        self._regressor = make_regressor()
        self._regressor.fit([h.as_row() for h in hikes], [h.duration_min for h in hikes])

    def predict(self, features: HikeFeatures) -> float:
        return float(self._regressor.predict([features.as_row()])[0])

# Killedar · किल्लेदार

*The keeper of a Maratha fort — this one fits in your pocket and works where the network doesn't.*

An offline trek companion for Sahyadri forts near Pune. Plan at home in a minute, then put the
phone away. On the fort, with no signal, ask questions and hear the fort's story — answered by
**Gemma running on your phone**.

Built for the [DEV Hacktoberfest 2026 Open-Source AI Challenge, Week 1: Touch Grass](https://dev.to/challenges/hacktoberfest-week1-2026-10-05).
Repository started **2026-10-10**.

## What it does

| Screen | Works offline | What happens |
|---|---|---|
| **Plan** | Partly | Pick a fort and trail. Killedar predicts *your* climb time from your past hikes (TabPFN) and works backwards from the last bus so you know when to leave Pune. Offline, it uses Naismith's rule. |
| **Ask** | Yes | Questions answered on-device by Gemma via WebLLM, grounded only in that fort's notes. English or Marathi. |
| **Listen** | Yes | Fort history read aloud — ElevenLabs narration bundled with the app, or the phone's own voice. |

## Why open models

The top of a Sahyadri fort usually has no signal, so a hosted API is useless exactly where you need
it. Open weights run on the phone, cost nothing per question, and your hiking history never leaves
your own server.

## Architecture

```
web/  PWA, zero runtime deps          api/  Starlette, online-only
  domain   pure rules, prompt           domain    features, Naismith baseline
  ports    LanguageModel, Predictor     ports     ClimbTimeModel
  app      planTrek, askFort            adapters  TabPFN, CSV, Naismith
  adapters WebLLM (Gemma), HTTP, data   app       /predict, /health
  ui       Plan / Ask / Listen
  service worker → shell, forts, audio precached; WebLLM caches model weights
```

Ports-and-adapters on both sides, with dependencies pointing inward. See [CLAUDE.md](CLAUDE.md) for the rules.

## Run it

```bash
# web — Node 22.18+
cd web && npm install && npm run check && npm run serve      # http://localhost:5173

# api — Python 3.11+
cd api && python -m venv .venv && . .venv/bin/activate
pip install -r requirements-dev.txt
python -m unittest discover -s tests -t .
uvicorn killedar_api.main:app --port 8000
# then build the web app against it:
cd ../web && KILLEDAR_API_URL=http://localhost:8000 npm run build
```

On a phone: open the deployed site in Chrome on Wi-Fi → Plan → **Download trail guide** →
switch to airplane mode → Ask.

### Your own hikes

Export past hikes (Strava, Google Fit, GPX) into `api/data/hikes.csv`:

```
distance_km,elevation_gain_m,start_hour,group_size,duration_min
3.0,600,7,2,118
```

`duration_min` is trailhead → summit. You need at least 8 rows; 20+ is better. Then compare models:

```bash
python -m killedar_api.evaluation data/hikes.csv
```

`data/hikes.sample.csv` is **synthetic** (generated by `data/make_sample.py`) so the API runs out of the box.
`data/hikes.csv` is currently **synthetic too** (`python data/make_sample.py --trails`: the fake hiker
climbing the app's real fort trails) — a placeholder until real hikes replace it.

### Narration

```bash
ELEVENLABS_API_KEY=… ELEVENLABS_VOICE_ID=… npm run audio
```

## Fort data

`web/public/forts/*.json` was written from the cited public sources (Wikipedia, linked in each file)
and is marked `"verified": false`. Bus and train times are deliberately left blank; the app asks you
for them. Please confirm details locally before relying on them, and send corrections.

## Deploy

`render.yaml` is a Render Blueprint: a static site for `web/` and a Python web service for `api/`.
TabPFN on CPU may need more than the free tier's 512 MB of memory.

## Built with

[Gemma](https://ai.google.dev/gemma) · [WebLLM](https://github.com/mlc-ai/web-llm) ·
[TabPFN](https://github.com/PriorLabs/TabPFN) · [ElevenLabs](https://elevenlabs.io) ·
[Starlette](https://www.starlette.io) · [Render](https://render.com)
<!-- TODO: demo video. Suggested 60–90 s shot list:
  1. Plan screen on Wi-Fi: pick Rajgad → enter last bus → "Leave Pune by 06:10" (10 s)
  2. Tap "Download trail guide", progress bar (cut; 5 s)
  3. Swipe down → airplane mode ON, clearly visible (5 s)
  4. Ask: "Is there water at the top?" → answer streams in (15 s)
  5. Switch to मराठी, ask the same → Marathi answer (15 s)
  6. Listen: history narration playing, camera pans to the actual fort if you have the footage (15 s)
-->
{% embed VIDEO_URL %}

**Try it:** [killedar.onrender.com](https://killedar.onrender.com) <!-- TODO: confirm final URL -->.
Use Chrome on Android or desktop; Ask needs WebGPU.

## Code

{% github abhijeetkaze/killedar %}

Two halves, both ports-and-adapters with a pure domain at the centre:

```
web/  PWA, zero runtime deps          api/  Starlette, online-only, optional
  domain   timing, prompt, model pick   domain    features, Naismith baseline
  ports    LanguageModel, Predictor     ports     ClimbTimeModel
  app      planTrek, askFort            adapters  TabPFN, CSV, Naismith
  adapters WebLLM (Gemma), HTTP, data   app       /predict, /health
```

<!-- TODO: update counts if they change --> 73 web tests and 30 API tests. CI runs both on every push.

## How I Built It

### Gemma, on the phone

The Ask screen runs Gemma through [WebLLM](https://github.com/mlc-ai/web-llm), which compiles
models to WebGPU. WebLLM is imported from a CDN at runtime, so the web app has **no runtime
dependencies**: TypeScript compiles straight to ES modules and there's no bundler.

Which Gemma? That depends on the phone, so the choice is a small pure function. It takes the newest
generation that fits under ~2.6B parameters, uses q4f16 if the GPU supports `shader-f16` (half
the memory of q4f32), and avoids WebLLM's `-1k` builds, because the fort notes plus the question
don't fit in 1,024 tokens. On a phone with f16 support that lands on **Gemma 3 1B (q4f16), about
700 MB of VRAM**. Without f16 it falls back to Gemma 2 2B in q4f32. I tested the picker against the
real model list WebLLM ships, not a hand-written one.

Small models make things up, so the prompt is built to keep the answers short and true:

- The fort data is rendered as **compact prose notes**, not JSON. Small models follow prose better,
  and it saves context.
- The instruction says *answer only from the notes; if they don't cover it, say so*, and **never
  invent bus times, distances or phone numbers**. On a mountain, a confident wrong answer is worse
  than "I don't know".
- Answers are capped at about 80 words, because the reader is walking.
- Gemma's chat template has no system role, so instruction, notes and question go in one user turn.

A service worker precaches the app shell, the fort JSON and the narration audio, and keeps the
WebLLM module after the first visit. WebLLM stores the weights in Cache Storage itself. Together
they make the Ask screen work in airplane mode.

### TabPFN: a model of *me*, from 20 rows

Naismith's rule (an hour per 5 km plus an hour per 600 m of climb) is the classic estimate, and it
was written for Scottish hills, not for a laterite staircase at 9 a.m. in October humidity. The useful
question isn't "how long does Rajgad take" but "how long does Rajgad take **me**".

That's a regression problem with almost no data: my own hike history, a few dozen rows at best.
It's exactly the case [TabPFN](https://github.com/PriorLabs/TabPFN) is made for. TabPFN is a
pre-trained tabular foundation model, so "fitting" it on 20 rows is in-context learning. There's no
training loop and nothing to overfit with hyperparameters.

Features: distance, elevation gain, start hour, group size. Target: trailhead-to-summit minutes.
The evaluation is leave-one-out, so each hike is predicted by a model that never saw it:

<!-- TODO: paste output of `python -m killedar_api.evaluation data/hikes.csv` on your real hikes -->
| | Mean absolute error (leave-one-out, N hikes) |
|---|---|
| Naismith's rule | **XX min** |
| TabPFN on my hikes | **XX min** |

<!-- TODO: one honest sentence interpreting it, e.g. "Naismith thinks I'm faster than I am on steep
ground; TabPFN noticed." If TabPFN didn't win, say so; that's a result too. -->

The API is deliberately **optional**. Prediction happens at home while you plan. If the service is
down or you're offline, the Plan screen falls back to Naismith locally and tells you so. It never
blocks.

### Facts about real places

Fort data is facts about real mountains, and wrong facts there have consequences. Every fort file
cites its sources and stays `"verified": false` until it's been checked. Bus times are **left blank
on purpose**: the app asks you for the last bus rather than guessing one, because rural ST timings
change and a hallucinated 6:30 p.m. bus is how people end up walking down in the dark.

### Narration

The Listen screen plays ElevenLabs narration bundled into the app at build time (`npm run audio`),
so it costs nothing on the fort and needs no signal. Without the audio files it falls back to the
phone's own speech synthesis.
<!-- TODO: delete the ElevenLabs sentence (and prize line below) if you didn't generate audio -->

### Deploy

One `render.yaml` blueprint deploys both halves to Render: the PWA as a static site and the
prediction API as a Python web service.

## Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

Because the top of a Sahyadri fort has no signal, and that settles the argument.

A closed model behind an API is a service. It's there when the network is, when the bill is paid,
and when the provider still offers it. On Rajgad's Balekilla none of those hold. Open weights are
an **artifact**: once they're on the phone, nobody can switch them off, rate-limit them or price them
per question.

Running on the device also keeps things private. My hike history (where I go, when, how slowly)
trains a model on my own server and goes nowhere else. Questions asked on the fort never leave the
phone at all.

It also matters who gets to build. Everything in Killedar is open: Gemma's weights, WebLLM's
compiler, TabPFN's model, the fort notes and their sources. So a trekking group in Nashik can fork
it, add Harishchandragad, correct my Marathi, and ship their own version without asking anyone's
permission or paying for anyone's API. Forts were built to stand on their own when cut off. The tool

# Render Blueprint: the PWA as a static site. That's the whole deployment — Gemma runs on the
# phone, and TabPFN's predictions are precomputed into web/public/predictions.json.

services:
  - type: web
    name: killedar
    runtime: static
    rootDir: web
    buildCommand: npm install && npm run build
    staticPublishPath: dist
    headers:
      - path: /sw.js
        name: Cache-Control
        value: no-cache

9	Built for the [DEV Hacktoberfest 2026 Open-Source AI Challenge, Week 1: Touch Grass](https://dev.to/challenges/hacktoberfest-week1-2026-10-05).
10	Repository started **2026-10-10**.
11	
12	## What it does
13	
14	| Screen | Works offline | What happens |
15	|---|---|---|
16	| **Plan** | Yes | Pick a fort and trail. Killedar predicts *your* climb time from your past hikes (TabPFN, precomputed) and works backwards from the last bus so you know when to leave Pune. |
17	| **Ask** | Yes | Questions answered on-device by Gemma via WebLLM, grounded only in that fort's notes. English or Marathi. |
18	| **Listen** | Yes | Fort history read aloud — ElevenLabs narration bundled with the app, or the phone's own voice. |
19	
20	## Why open models
21	
22	The top of a Sahyadri fort usually has no signal, so a hosted API is useless exactly where you need
23	it. Open weights run on the phone, cost nothing per question, and your hiking history never leaves
24	your own laptop. There is no backend at all.
25	
26	## Architecture
27	
28	```
29	web/  PWA, zero runtime deps             api/  Python tooling, run on your laptop
30	  domain   pure rules, prompt, table       domain     features, Naismith baseline
31	  ports    LanguageModel, Predictor        adapters   TabPFN, hikes CSV, fort trails
32	  app      planTrek, askFort               evaluation leave-one-out vs Naismith
33	  adapters WebLLM (Gemma), table, data     precompute → web/public/predictions.json
34	  ui       Plan / Ask / Listen
35	  service worker → shell, forts, predictions, audio precached; WebLLM caches model weights
36	```
37	
38	Gemma runs in the browser. TabPFN can't, but the app only asks about its own trails at a start
39	hour (4–14) and group size (1–30), so `precompute` answers all ~1,650 questions ahead of time
40	into a 7 KB JSON file that ships with the app.
41	
42	Ports-and-adapters on both sides, with dependencies pointing inward. See [CLAUDE.md](CLAUDE.md) for the rules.
43	
44	## Run it
45	
46	```bash
47	# web — Node 22.18+
48	cd web && npm install && npm run check && npm run serve      # http://localhost:5173
49	
50	# api — Python 3.11+
51	cd api && python -m venv .venv && . .venv/bin/activate
52	pip install -r requirements-dev.txt
53	python -m unittest discover -s tests -t .
54	```
55	
56	On a phone: open the deployed site in Chrome on Wi-Fi → Plan → **Download trail guide** →
57	switch to airplane mode → Ask.
58	
59	### Your own hikes
60	
61	Export past hikes (Strava, Google Fit, GPX) into `api/data/hikes.csv`:
62	
63	```
64	distance_km,elevation_gain_m,start_hour,group_size,duration_min
65	3.0,600,7,2,118
66	```
67	
68	`duration_min` is trailhead → summit. You need at least 8 rows; 20+ is better. Then compare models
69	and regenerate the app's predictions:
70	
71	```bash
72	python -m killedar_api.evaluation data/hikes.csv
73	python -m killedar_api.precompute data/hikes.csv   # → web/public/predictions.json; commit it
74	```
75	
76	`data/hikes.sample.csv` is **synthetic** (generated by `data/make_sample.py`) for the tests.
77	`data/hikes.csv` is currently **synthetic too** (`python data/make_sample.py --trails`: the fake hiker
78	climbing the app's real fort trails) — a placeholder until real hikes replace it.
79	
80	### Narration
81	
82	```bash
83	ELEVENLABS_API_KEY=… ELEVENLABS_VOICE_ID=… npm run audio
84	```
...
83	## Fort data
84	
85	`web/public/forts/*.json` was written from the cited public sources (Wikipedia, linked in each file)
86	and is marked `"verified": false`. Bus and train times are deliberately left blank; the app asks you
87	for them. Please confirm details locally before relying on them, and send corrections.
88	
89	## Deploy
90	
91	`render.yaml` is a Render Blueprint for one static site (`web/`). That's the whole deployment.
92	
93	## Built with
94	
95	[Gemma](https://ai.google.dev/gemma) · [WebLLM](https://github.com/mlc-ai/web-llm) ·
96	[TabPFN](https://github.com/PriorLabs/TabPFN) · [ElevenLabs](https://elevenlabs.io) ·
97	[Render](https://render.com)

content.text:
The backend is gone and the live site works offline with TabPFN predictions. I tested it in headless Chrome:

| | Before | Now |
|---|---|---|
| Plan screen, online | Hung ~25 s on the crashing API, then showed the rule of thumb. | **21 ms**: "Climb about 2 h 3 min at your pace, 31 min slower than the rule of thumb." |
| Plan screen, offline | Rule of thumb only. | **23 ms**, same TabPFN estimate. |

CI passed and Render redeployed the site.

**How it works now:** TabPFN runs once on your laptop and answers every question the Plan screen can ask: 5 trails × start hours 4–14 × groups of 1–30. The answers go into a 7 KB `predictions.json` that the service worker caches with the app. Gemma still runs on the phone, so the whole app is one static site. Anything outside the table, such as a new trail, falls back to Naismith.

Three commits, all pushed:
- **API:** the server, `/predict` and Starlette are gone, replaced by a `precompute` script. 23 Python tests pass, including the real-TabPFN one.
- **Web:** a table predictor replaces the HTTP one. 75 tests pass, including one that checks the shipped `predictions.json` covers every fort trail.
- **Deploy and docs:** [render.yaml](render.yaml) is now one static site. CI runs evaluation and precompute with the real TabPFN. The README, CLAUDE.md and [the post](docs/dev-post.md) are updated, and the post now uses the required `#hf26challenge` tag. I added a short paragraph to the post about why the API was dropped; it's true and makes a good story.

**What you need to do:**
1. **Delete the `killedar-api` service** in the Render dashboard. Removing it from `render.yaml` doesn't delete the running service.
2. **Replace the synthetic hikes.** Once `api/data/hikes.csv` has real hikes, run:
   ```bash
   cd api && . .venv/bin/activate
   python -m killedar_api.evaluation data/hikes.csv   # numbers for the post
   python -m killedar_api.precompute data/hikes.csv   # then commit web/public/predictions.json
   ```
   Until then, the post's TabPFN numbers must stay as placeholders or be labelled synthetic.
3. **Record the demo** on a real phone. WebGPU doesn't run headless, so I couldn't test Gemma itself.

The Render category is weaker now: Render only hosts the front end, which the rules allow ("host an agent's front end"). Everything else gets stronger, because the whole app works in airplane mode.

The offline setup is built, committed and pushed. All 88 web tests pass. Render redeploys on push; I didn't wait for it.

**How it works:**
- **A "Use offline" button** with a cloud icon sits next to "Sinhagad, 1,312 m" on every screen. Using offline is opt-in.
- **Tapping it opens a "Use Killedar with no signal" panel** with two steps, each with its own icon, progress bar and status:
  1. *App, fort notes and your climb times*: under 1 MB, with a "12 of 36 files" count.
  2. *Gemma trail guide, for Ask*: about 0.7–1.5 GB, with WebLLM's download progress.
- **"Download for offline"** runs both steps. The header button turns into a progress ring with "Saving 42%", and keeps updating if you close the panel or switch screens.
- **When it finishes**, the button turns green ("✓ Offline ready") and the panel says "Ready for the fort. Turn on airplane mode and try it." The app also asks the browser not to delete the saved files when space runs low.
- **If something fails**, the step is marked and the button changes to "Try again".
- **Without WebGPU**, as on your machine, the files still save and the panel explains how to enable Ask. Plan and Listen still work offline.
- **If you tap Ask before downloading the guide**, the panel opens.

**Tested in headless Chrome at phone width:** "Use offline" → download → "Offline ready", and it stays ready after reloading with the network off. I fixed two layout problems found in the screenshots: the button was squeezing the fort picker, and the panel's buttons wrapped. The Gemma download step itself, including its progress ring, I couldn't test here because headless Chrome has no GPU. It needs testing on your phone.

**To try it locally:** http://localhost:5173 is still running the latest build. Reload twice, because the old service worker serves the previous version once. To see the Gemma step on your desktop, enable `chrome://flags/#enable-unsafe-webgpu` and `#enable-vulkan`, then restart Chrome.

The demo shot list in [docs/dev-post.md](docs/dev-post.md) now uses this flow. The green "Offline ready" check followed by airplane mode makes a good shot for the video.

I won't add that token to the app. Here's why, and where a token would actually help:

- **Anything in the PWA is public.** The app runs in every visitor's browser and the repo is public, so the token would be readable by anyone who opens DevTools or the GitHub repo. People can abuse a leaked token under your account.
- **It wouldn't help the app anyway.** WebLLM downloads Gemma from the public `mlc-ai` repos on Hugging Face, which don't need a token. Each user downloads it once, from their own IP, so per-user rate limits aren't a concern.
- **It would help in CI.** CI downloads the TabPFN weights from Hugging Face on every run. If you want, I can store the token as a GitHub Actions secret (`gh secret set HF_TOKEN`) and pass it to that job only. It stays encrypted and is never in the repo. Tell me if you want that.

You've pasted the token into this chat, so consider regenerating it at huggingface.co/settings/tokens. That's cautious rather than urgent, since it hasn't been committed anywhere.

content.text:
I found and fixed two real bugs in the Gemma download that Ask depends on. That should fix the stuck download. If Ask still fails on your machine, the earlier WebGPU message points to your browser setup, not the app.

I couldn't run a full download to the end: the test browser allows only 778 MB of storage, so I haven't seen Gemma answer a question.

**What I tested:** headless Chrome with a software GPU, running Ask and then the full download.
- **Ask, before downloading:** works as designed. It says the guide isn't on the phone yet and opens the offline panel.
- **The download itself:** starts fine. About 1.4 GB arrives in 42 parts from Hugging Face, with no errors or rate limits, and the progress ring updates.

**The bugs:**
1. **Running out of storage froze the panel at "Saving 52%".** The download stopped with a `QuotaExceededError`, but WebLLM kept sending progress updates afterwards, and those overwrote the failure. The app now ignores updates after the download has finished or failed.
2. **The failure message was unclear.** It now reads "Not enough storage for the guide. Free up about 1.5 GB (and don't use a private/incognito window), then try again." The long WebLLM progress text is also shortened. Five new tests cover these, and all 92 web tests pass. Pushed in `72640ff`.

**Why Ask may still fail on your machine:** the earlier "WebGPU is present but no GPU adapter is available" message means your Chrome has WebGPU switched off for your GPU. Without WebGPU, Gemma can't run there at all. To fix it:
1. Open `chrome://flags`, enable **#enable-unsafe-webgpu** and **#enable-vulkan**, and restart Chrome.
2. Check `chrome://gpu`. WebGPU should say "Hardware accelerated".
3. Don't use an incognito window, which gets the small storage limit I hit.
4. Reload http://localhost:5173 twice, tap **Use offline** → **Download for offline**, and wait for the green check.

If it still fails, open DevTools (F12) → Console and send me the lines starting with `[Killedar]`. Every failure now logs its real cause there.

The simplest real test is still Chrome on an Android phone, where WebGPU is on by default. If the GPU lacks the f16 feature, as here, the app falls back to the larger Gemma 2 2B (about 1.4 GB). Phones with f16 get Gemma 3 1B (about 0.7 GB).

content.text:
I found the cause of the Ask error and fixed it, but the fix is only committed locally (`d758a36`), not pushed yet. Gemma 3 1B can't run in my test setup, so it isn't confirmed working until you try it.

**Cause:** Gemma 3 1B's config, as WebLLM downloads it, sets both a context window (8,192 tokens) and a 512-token "sliding window". WebLLM 0.2.85 refuses to start a model when both are positive. It's a packaging mismatch between WebLLM and that model, not something in our prompt or code.

**Fix:** the 512-token window is Gemma 3's local attention, and the model reads it from its own settings. So when the app starts the engine, it now switches the duplicate engine-level setting off and asks for a 4,096-token context explicitly. The change is a small function in [model.ts](web/src/domain/model.ts) plus one argument in the WebLLM adapter. Two new tests cover it, and all 94 web tests pass.

**Still running in the background:** a full Gemma 2 2B download and Ask on a software GPU. It checks that the new settings don't break the fallback model, and it's slow, so it may take several minutes. Your browser downloads the Gemma 3 1B version, which this test environment can't run because it has no f16 support. Once it passes, I'll push.

**When it's pushed:** reload http://localhost:5173 twice and tap Ask. The model is already downloaded, so it should go straight from "Waking up the guide…" to an answer. If anything fails, the console will show a `[Killedar]` line with the reason.

content.text:
The repeated "- Sinhagad" answer came from my previous fix, and the only way around it is switching to the larger Gemma 2 2B. The repeating is gone in theory, but I couldn't run either model here, so it needs your test. The server is already serving the new build. Both commits (`d758a36`, `923b826`) are local only.

**Why Gemma 3 1B can't work here:** Gemma 3 has some layers that look back only 512 tokens and others that see everything. WebLLM 0.2.85 can only set one attention window for the whole model:
- **Window off** (my earlier fix): the short-range layers see the whole ~2,000-token fort prompt, which they were never trained on, and the output collapses into the same line repeated.
- **Window on** (WebLLM's default): every layer forgets everything older than the last 512 tokens, including the fort notes.

So no setting gives Gemma 3 1B correct answers with our prompt.

**The change:** the app now uses **Gemma 2 2B**, the lightest Gemma that works in this version of WebLLM. Its short-range window is the same size as its full context (4,096 tokens), so it's unaffected. It's also likely better at Marathi.

The trade-off is a bigger download: **about 1.5 GB instead of 0.6 GB**, once. You wanted the lightest model, but no lighter Gemma works here. The offline panel's size text and the DEV post now say so. The post also tells this story briefly, which suits the "Writing quality" judging. All 95 tests pass.

**To test:**
1. Reload twice.
2. Tap **Use offline** → **Download for offline**. Gemma 2 isn't downloaded yet, so it's a new ~1.5 GB download.
3. Ask "What happened here in history?" on Sinhagad.

The 600 MB of Gemma 3 is still stored in the browser. To free that space, go to DevTools → Application → Storage → **Clear site data** before step 2. It also clears the app's other saved data, which is fine because step 2 re-saves everything.

Tell me how Ask behaves and I'll push both commits.

content.text:
The key was only used once, on your laptop, while I generated the audio. The app itself never contacts ElevenLabs.

**How the key was used:**

I ran the generator script once with the key passed in as a temporary setting for that one command:
```bash
ELEVENLABS_API_KEY=sk_… ELEVENLABS_VOICE_ID=JBFqnCBsd6RMkjVDRZzb npm run audio
```
[generate-audio.ts](web/scripts/generate-audio.ts) reads it from `process.env.ELEVENLABS_API_KEY`, and it went out only in the `xi-api-key` header of 6 requests to `api.elevenlabs.io`. Each request sent one fort's history text and got back an MP3. The script saved those as `web/public/audio/*.mp3`.

The setting disappeared when the command finished. It isn't in any file, in your git config or in the shell profile.

**What ships to users:**

Only the six MP3 files, which are committed like images. When someone opens Listen, the app plays `audio/sinhagad-mr.mp3` from its own files. That's why it works on the fort with no signal and costs you no ElevenLabs credits per listen.

```
your laptop (once)                         user's phone (every time)
──────────────────                         ─────────────────────────
history text ──► ElevenLabs API ──► .mp3 ──► committed ──► Listen plays the .mp3
                 (key used here)                           (no key, no network)
```

**When you need the key again:**

Only to regenerate the clips, for example after editing a fort's history or choosing another voice:
```bash
cd web
ELEVENLABS_API_KEY=your_key ELEVENLABS_VOICE_ID=voice_id npm run audio -- --force
```

I deliberately left it out of the app. Anything in the PWA is downloadable by every visitor, so a key there would let anyone spend your ElevenLabs credits. I also didn't save it anywhere in the repo.
ok how will be prove to judge that we used eleven labs api key

You never show the key itself. Judges can't verify a key, and publishing one would let anyone spend your credits. What they look for is evidence that the project uses ElevenLabs, and that's all public in the repo and the app:

| Evidence | Where a judge sees it |
|---|---|
| **The code that calls the API** | [web/scripts/generate-audio.ts](web/scripts/generate-audio.ts): a `POST` to `api.elevenlabs.io/v1/text-to-speech/…` using model `eleven_v3` with a `language_code` per clip. |
| **The output** | `web/public/audio/*.mp3`: six committed clips in English and Marathi. The git history shows them added by the narration commit. |
| **It working in the app** | Listen on killedar.onrender.com plays them, with "Narration: ElevenLabs" under the player. |
| **The write-up** | The post's Narration section and its Best Use of ElevenLabs line, including the Marathi model finding. That kind of detail shows real use. |
| **The demo video** | Shot 6 of the shot list: Listen playing Marathi narration, ideally after switching on airplane mode. |

This matches the category wording, which counts *"generate narration for your demo"* as a valid use, so you're well covered.

Two ways to make it more convincing:
1. **Narrate the demo video itself with ElevenLabs.** Write a 60–90 s voiceover script, generate it with your key, and lay it over the screen recording. That's a second, very visible use, and it's literally the example the category gives. I can write the script and generate the MP3 if you want.

1	---
2	title: "Killedar: a fort guide that works where the signal dies"
3	published: false
4	tags: devchallenge, hf26challenge, opensource, ai
5	cover_image: <!-- TODO: trek photo URL (upload to DEV first) -->
6	---
7	
8	*This is a submission for the [DEV Hacktoberfest 2026 Open-Source AI Challenge, Week 1: Touch Grass](https://dev.to/challenges/hacktoberfest-week1-2026-10-05).*
9	
10	<!-- TODO: trek photo — you on/near the fort, ideally with the phone visible -->
11	![On top of <FORT>, no bars](PHOTO_URL)
12	
13	## What I Built
14	
15	Halfway up Rajgad the bars on your phone go one by one. By Padmavati Machi you're carrying a
16	very expensive torch.
17	
18	<!-- TODO (2–3 sentences, your own): the moment this happened to you — which fort, what you wanted to
19	know and couldn't look up, or the last bus you nearly missed. Specifics beat adjectives. -->
20	
21	That's the problem with every AI trek assistant I could imagine building on a hosted API: it works
22	in Pune and stops working at the trailhead, which is exactly where you need it.
23	
24	**Killedar** (किल्लेदार, the keeper of a Maratha fort) is an offline trek companion for the
25	Sahyadri forts around Pune: Sinhagad, Rajgad and Lohagad to start. It's a PWA with three
26	screens:
27	
28	- **Plan**, at home, online: pick a fort and a trail and enter the last bus back from the base village.
29	  Killedar predicts *your* climb time from your own past hikes and works backwards from that bus,
30	  so it tells you when to leave Pune and not just how long the climb takes.
31	- **Ask**, on the fort, offline: "Is there water on Padmavati Machi?" "Which way is the Chor
32	  Darwaja route?" Answered by **Gemma running on the phone**, grounded only in that fort's notes,
33	  in English or Marathi.
34	- **Listen**, offline: the fort's history read aloud, so you can look at the walls instead of the screen.
35	
36	You download the trail guide once on Wi-Fi. After that, airplane mode is fine.
37	
38	## Demo
39	
40	<!-- TODO: demo video. Suggested 60–90 s shot list:
41	  1. Plan screen on Wi-Fi: pick Rajgad → enter last bus → "Leave Pune by 06:10" (10 s)
42	  2. Tap "Use offline" → "Download for offline": progress ring, then the green "Offline ready" check (cut; 5 s)
43	  3. Swipe down → airplane mode ON, clearly visible (5 s)
44	  4. Ask: "Is there water at the top?" → answer streams in (15 s)
45	  5. Switch to मराठी, ask the same → Marathi answer (15 s)
46	  6. Listen: history narration playing, camera pans to the actual fort if you have the footage (15 s)
47	-->
48	{% embed VIDEO_URL %}
49	
50	**Try it:** [killedar.onrender.com](https://killedar.onrender.com).
51	Use Chrome on Android or desktop; Ask needs WebGPU.
52	
53	## Code
54	
55	{% github abhijeetkaze/killedar %}
56	
57	A static PWA and a bit of Python I run on my laptop. **There is no backend.** Both halves are
58	ports-and-adapters with a pure domain at the centre:
59	
60	```
61	web/  PWA, zero runtime deps             api/  Python tooling, not a server
62	  domain   timing, prompt, model pick      domain     features, Naismith baseline
63	  ports    LanguageModel, Predictor        adapters   TabPFN, hikes CSV, fort trails
64	  app      planTrek, askFort               evaluation leave-one-out vs Naismith
65	  adapters WebLLM (Gemma), table, data     precompute → web/public/predictions.json
66	```
67	
68	<!-- TODO: update counts if they change --> 75 web tests and 23 Python tests. CI runs both on every
69	push, including the real TabPFN model.
70	
71	## How I Built It
72	
73	### Gemma, on the phone
74	
75	The Ask screen runs Gemma through [WebLLM](https://github.com/mlc-ai/web-llm), which compiles
76	models to WebGPU. WebLLM is imported from a CDN at runtime, so the web app has **no runtime
77	dependencies**: TypeScript compiles straight to ES modules and there's no bundler.
78	
79	Which Gemma? That depends on the phone, so the choice is a small pure function. It takes the newest
80	generation that fits under ~2.6B parameters, uses q4f16 if the GPU supports `shader-f16` (half
81	the memory of q4f32), and avoids WebLLM's `-1k` builds, because the fort notes plus the question
82	don't fit in 1,024 tokens. I tested the picker against the real model list WebLLM ships, not a
83	hand-written one.
84	
85	My first pick was **Gemma 3 1B**: newest and smallest, a 600 MB download. It loaded, and then
86	answered "What happened here in history?" with "- Sinhagad" fifty times. Gemma 3 mixes
87	512-token local-attention layers with global ones, and WebLLM 0.2 can give the model only one
88	attention window. Switch it off and the local layers read the whole ~2,000-token fort prompt they
89	were never trained on; switch it on and every layer forgets the fort notes after 512 tokens.
90	So Killedar runs **Gemma 2 2B (q4f16, about 1.5 GB, once)**, whose local window equals its context.
91	A bigger download, but answers you can trust on a mountain.
92	
93	Small models make things up, so the prompt is built to keep the answers short and true:
94	
95	- The fort data is rendered as **compact prose notes**, not JSON. Small models follow prose better,
96	  and it saves context.
97	- The instruction says *answer only from the notes; if they don't cover it, say so*, and **never
98	  invent bus times, distances or phone numbers**. On a mountain, a confident wrong answer is worse
99	  than "I don't know".
100	- Answers are capped at about 80 words, because the reader is walking.
101	- Gemma's chat template has no system role, so instruction, notes and question go in one user turn.
102	
103	A service worker precaches the app shell, the fort JSON and the narration audio, and keeps the
104	WebLLM module after the first visit. WebLLM stores the weights in Cache Storage itself. Together
105	they make the Ask screen work in airplane mode.
106	
107	### TabPFN: a model of *me*, from 20 rows
108	
109	Naismith's rule (an hour per 5 km plus an hour per 600 m of climb) is the classic estimate, and it
110	was written for Scottish hills, not for a laterite staircase at 9 a.m. in October humidity. The useful
111	question isn't "how long does Rajgad take" but "how long does Rajgad take **me**".
112	
113	That's a regression problem with almost no data: my own hike history, a few dozen rows at best.
114	It's exactly the case [TabPFN](https://github.com/PriorLabs/TabPFN) is made for. TabPFN is a
115	pre-trained tabular foundation model, so "fitting" it on 20 rows is in-context learning. There's no
116	training loop and nothing to overfit with hyperparameters.
117	
118	Features: distance, elevation gain, start hour, group size. Target: trailhead-to-summit minutes.
119	The evaluation is leave-one-out, so each hike is predicted by a model that never saw it:
120	
121	<!-- TODO: paste output of `python -m killedar_api.evaluation data/hikes.csv` on your real hikes -->
122	| | Mean absolute error (leave-one-out, N hikes) |
123	|---|---|
124	| Naismith's rule | **XX min** |
125	| TabPFN on my hikes | **XX min** |
126	
127	<!-- TODO: one honest sentence interpreting it, e.g. "Naismith thinks I'm faster than I am on steep
128	ground; TabPFN noticed." If TabPFN didn't win, say so; that's a result too. -->
129	
130	My first version served TabPFN from a small web API. It worked, but it was the wrong shape twice
131	over. It needed signal, which is the one thing this app can't assume. And PyTorch plus TabPFN sat
132	right at the 512 MB limit of a free instance, so every prediction knocked the server over.
133	
134	The fix was to notice how small the question space is. The app only ever asks about its own
135	trails, at a start hour between 4 and 14 and a group of 1 to 30. That's about 1,650 questions.
136	So TabPFN answers **all of them ahead of time**, on my laptop, in about 13 seconds:
137	
138	```bash
139	python -m killedar_api.precompute data/hikes.csv   # → web/public/predictions.json (7 KB)
140	```
141	
142	The service worker caches that file with the app shell. The Plan screen looks up *my* climb time in
143	about 20 ms, online or on the summit, and anything outside the table falls back to Naismith.
144	TabPFN still does the learning; the phone just reads its answers.
145	
146	### Facts about real places
147	
148	Fort data is facts about real mountains, and wrong facts there have consequences. Every fort file
149	cites its sources and stays `"verified": false` until it's been checked. Bus times are **left blank
150	on purpose**: the app asks you for the last bus rather than guessing one, because rural ST timings
151	change and a hallucinated 6:30 p.m. bus is how people end up walking down in the dark.
152	
153	### Narration
154	
155	The Listen screen plays ElevenLabs narration bundled into the app at build time (`npm run audio`):
156	each fort's history in English and in Marathi, six clips, 1.4 MB in all. They're precached with the

## What I Built

Halfway up Rajgad the bars on your phone go one by one. By Padmavati Machi you're carrying a
very expensive torch.

<!-- TODO (2–3 sentences, your own): the moment this happened to you — which fort, what you wanted to
know and couldn't look up, or the last bus you nearly missed. Specifics beat adjectives. -->

That's the problem with every AI trek assistant I could imagine building on a hosted API: it works
in Pune and stops working at the trailhead, which is exactly where you need it.

**Killedar** (किल्लेदार, the keeper of a Maratha fort) is an offline trek companion for the
Sahyadri forts around Pune: Sinhagad, Rajgad and Lohagad to start. It's a PWA with three
screens:

- **Plan**, at home, online: pick a fort and a trail and enter the last bus back from the base village.
  Killedar predicts *your* climb time from your own past hikes and works backwards from that bus,
  so it tells you when to leave Pune and not just how long the climb takes.
- **Ask**, on the fort, offline: "Is there water on Padmavati Machi?" "Which way is the Chor
  Darwaja route?" Answered by **Gemma running on the phone**, grounded only in that fort's notes,
  in English or Marathi.
- **Listen**, offline: the fort's history read aloud, so you can look at the walls instead of the screen.

You download the trail guide once on Wi-Fi. After that, airplane mode is fine.

## Demo

<!-- TODO: demo video. Suggested 60–90 s shot list:
  1. Plan screen on Wi-Fi: pick Rajgad → enter last bus → "Leave Pune by 06:10" (10 s)
  2. Tap "Use offline" → "Download for offline": progress ring, then the green "Offline ready" check (cut; 5 s)
  3. Swipe down → airplane mode ON, clearly visible (5 s)
  4. Ask: "Is there water at the top?" → answer streams in (15 s)
  5. Switch to मराठी, ask the same → Marathi answer (15 s)
  6. Listen: history narration playing, camera pans to the actual fort if you have the footage (15 s)
-->
{% embed VIDEO_URL %}

**Try it:** [killedar.onrender.com](https://killedar.onrender.com).
Use Chrome on Android or desktop; Ask needs WebGPU.

## Code

{% github abhijeetkaze/killedar %}

A static PWA and a bit of Python I run on my laptop. **There is no backend.** Both halves are
ports-and-adapters with a pure domain at the centre:

```
web/  PWA, zero runtime deps             api/  Python tooling, not a server
  domain   timing, prompt, model pick      domain     features, Naismith baseline
  ports    LanguageModel, Predictor        adapters   TabPFN, hikes CSV, fort trails
  app      planTrek, askFort               evaluation leave-one-out vs Naismith
  adapters WebLLM (Gemma), table, data     precompute → web/public/predictions.json
```

<!-- TODO: update counts if they change --> 75 web tests and 23 Python tests. CI runs both on every
push, including the real TabPFN model.

## How I Built It

### Gemma, on the phone

The Ask screen runs Gemma through [WebLLM](https://github.com/mlc-ai/web-llm), which compiles
models to WebGPU. WebLLM is imported from a CDN at runtime, so the web app has **no runtime
dependencies**: TypeScript compiles straight to ES modules and there's no bundler.

Which Gemma? That depends on the phone, so the choice is a small pure function. It takes the newest
generation that fits under ~2.6B parameters, uses q4f16 if the GPU supports `shader-f16` (half
the memory of q4f32), and avoids WebLLM's `-1k` builds, because the fort notes plus the question
don't fit in 1,024 tokens. I tested the picker against the real model list WebLLM ships, not a
hand-written one.

My first pick was **Gemma 3 1B**: newest and smallest, a 600 MB download. It loaded, and then
answered "What happened here in history?" with "- Sinhagad" fifty times. Gemma 3 mixes
512-token local-attention layers with global ones, and WebLLM 0.2 can give the model only one
attention window. Switch it off and the local layers read the whole ~2,000-token fort prompt they
were never trained on; switch it on and every layer forgets the fort notes after 512 tokens.
So Killedar runs **Gemma 2 2B (q4f16, about 1.5 GB, once)**, whose local window equals its context.
A bigger download, but answers you can trust on a mountain.

Small models make things up, so the prompt is built to keep the answers short and true:

- The fort data is rendered as **compact prose notes**, not JSON. Small models follow prose better,
  and it saves context.
- The instruction says *answer only from the notes; if they don't cover it, say so*, and **never
  invent bus times, distances or phone numbers**. On a mountain, a confident wrong answer is worse
  than "I don't know".
- Answers are capped at about 80 words, because the reader is walking.
- Gemma's chat template has no system role, so instruction, notes and question go in one user turn.

A service worker precaches the app shell, the fort JSON and the narration audio, and keeps the
WebLLM module after the first visit. WebLLM stores the weights in Cache Storage itself. Together
they make the Ask screen work in airplane mode.

### TabPFN: a model of *me*, from 20 rows

Naismith's rule (an hour per 5 km plus an hour per 600 m of climb) is the classic estimate, and it
was written for Scottish hills, not for a laterite staircase at 9 a.m. in October humidity. The useful
question isn't "how long does Rajgad take" but "how long does Rajgad take **me**".

That's a regression problem with almost no data: my own hike history, a few dozen rows at best.
It's exactly the case [TabPFN](https://github.com/PriorLabs/TabPFN) is made for. TabPFN is a
pre-trained tabular foundation model, so "fitting" it on 20 rows is in-context learning. There's no
training loop and nothing to overfit with hyperparameters.

Features: distance, elevation gain, start hour, group size. Target: trailhead-to-summit minutes.
The evaluation is leave-one-out, so each hike is predicted by a model that never saw it:

<!-- TODO: paste output of `python -m killedar_api.evaluation data/hikes.csv` on your real hikes -->
| | Mean absolute error (leave-one-out, N hikes) |
|---|---|
| Naismith's rule | **XX min** |
| TabPFN on my hikes | **XX min** |

<!-- TODO: one honest sentence interpreting it, e.g. "Naismith thinks I'm faster than I am on steep
ground; TabPFN noticed." If TabPFN didn't win, say so; that's a result too. -->

My first version served TabPFN from a small web API. It worked, but it was the wrong shape twice
over. It needed signal, which is the one thing this app can't assume. And PyTorch plus TabPFN sat
right at the 512 MB limit of a free instance, so every prediction knocked the server over.

trails, at a start hour between 4 and 14 and a group of 1 to 30. That's about 1,650 questions.
So TabPFN answers **all of them ahead of time**, on my laptop, in about 13 seconds:

```bash
python -m killedar_api.precompute data/hikes.csv   # → web/public/predictions.json (7 KB)
```

The service worker caches that file with the app shell. The Plan screen looks up *my* climb time in
about 20 ms, online or on the summit, and anything outside the table falls back to Naismith.
TabPFN still does the learning; the phone just reads its answers.

### Facts about real places

Fort data is facts about real mountains, and wrong facts there have consequences. Every fort file
cites its sources and stays `"verified": false` until it's been checked. Bus times are **left blank
on purpose**: the app asks you for the last bus rather than guessing one, because rural ST timings
change and a hallucinated 6:30 p.m. bus is how people end up walking down in the dark.

The Listen screen plays ElevenLabs narration bundled into the app at build time (`npm run audio`):
each fort's history in English and in Marathi, six clips, 1.4 MB in all. They're precached with the
app, so they cost nothing on the fort and need no signal. Marathi was the catch: the usual
`eleven_multilingual_v2` model rejects it outright, so the script uses `eleven_v3` and sends each
clip's language code. A fort with no clip falls back to the phone's own speech synthesis.

One `render.yaml` blueprint deploys the PWA to Render as a static site. That's the whole
deployment: Gemma runs on the phone, and TabPFN's answers ship in a 7 KB file.

Because the top of a Sahyadri fort has no signal, and that settles the argument.

A closed model behind an API is a service. It's there when the network is, when the bill is paid,
and when the provider still offers it. On Rajgad's Balekilla none of those hold. Open weights are
an **artifact**: once they're on the phone, nobody can switch them off, rate-limit them or price them
per question.

Running on the device also keeps things private. My hike history (where I go, when, how slowly)
goes into TabPFN on my own laptop, and only the predicted minutes ship with the app. Questions asked on the fort never leave the
phone at all.

It also matters who gets to build. Everything in Killedar is open: Gemma's weights, WebLLM's
compiler, TabPFN's model, the fort notes and their sources. So a trekking group in Nashik can fork
it, add Harishchandragad, correct my Marathi, and ship their own version without asking anyone's
permission or paying for anyone's API. Forts were built to stand on their own when cut off. The tool
for climbing them should too.
