- **Best Use of Gemma**: Gemma 2 2B runs entirely on the phone via WebLLM and
  answers questions offline in English and Marathi, grounded in cited fort notes.
- **Best Use of TabPFN**: a personal climb-time model fitted in-context on a few dozen of my own
  hikes, evaluated leave-one-out against Naismith's rule (numbers above), and precomputed so its
  predictions work offline on the fort.
- **Best Use of Render**: Render hosts the app's front end, a static site deployed from one
  `render.yaml` blueprint. All the AI runs on the phone.
- **Best Use of ElevenLabs**: fort histories narrated at build time and bundled offline, so they
  play on the summit with no signal, in English and Marathi (`eleven_v3`).

---

*Built solo in Pune, October 2026. Fort data is unverified. Check locally before you climb, and
send corrections.* <!-- TODO: team/credits line if anyone helped -->

title: "Killedar: a fort guide that works where the signal dies"
published: false

*This is a submission for the [DEV Hacktoberfest 2026 Open-Source AI Challenge, Week 1: Touch Grass](https://dev.to/challenges/hacktoberfest-week1-2026-10-05).*

<!-- TODO: trek photo — you on/near the fort, ideally with the phone visible -->
![On top of <FORT>, no bars](PHOTO_URL)

## What I Built

Halfway up Rajgad the bars on your phone go one by one. By Padmavati Machi you're carrying a
very expensive torch.

<!-- TODO (2–3 sentences, your own): the moment this happened to you — which fort, what you wanted to
know and couldn't look up, or the last bus you nearly missed. Specifics beat adjectives. -->

That's the problem with every AI trek assistant I could imagine building on a hosted API: it works
in Pune and stops working at the trailhead, which is exactly where you need it.

**Killedar** (किल्लेदार, the keeper of a Maratha fort) is an offline trek companion for the
Sahyadri forts around Pune: Sinhagad, Rajgad and Lohagad to start. It's a PWA with three
screens, and all three work in airplane mode:

- **Plan**: pick a fort and a trail and enter the last bus back from the base village. Killedar
  predicts *your* climb time from your own past hikes and works backwards from that bus, so it
  tells you when to leave Pune and not just how long the climb takes.
- **Ask**: "Is there water on Padmavati Machi?" "Is the Chor Darwaja route OK for beginners?"
  Answered by **Gemma running on the phone**, grounded only in that fort's notes, in English or
  Marathi.
- **Listen**: the fort's history read aloud in English or Marathi, so you can look at the walls
  instead of the screen.

On Wi-Fi at home you tap **Use offline** once. Killedar saves the app, the fort notes, your
predicted climb times, the narration and the Gemma model, shows the progress, and turns green when
it's ready. After that, airplane mode is fine.

## Demo

<!-- TODO: demo video. Suggested 60–90 s shot list:
  1. Plan screen on Wi-Fi: pick Rajgad → enter last bus → "Leave Pune by 06:10" (10 s)
  2. Tap "Use offline" → "Download for offline": progress ring, then the green "Offline ready" check (cut; 5 s)
  3. Swipe down → airplane mode ON, clearly visible (5 s)
  4. Ask: "Is there water on Padmavati Machi?" → answer streams in (15 s)
  5. Switch to मराठी, ask the same → Marathi answer (15 s)
  6. Listen: Marathi narration playing, camera pans to the actual fort if you have the footage (15 s)
-->
{% embed VIDEO_URL %}

**Try it:** [killedar.onrender.com](https://killedar.onrender.com). Plan and Listen work in any
modern browser. Ask needs WebGPU: Chrome on Android, or desktop Chrome with a supported GPU.

## Code

{% github abhijeetkaze/killedar %}

A static PWA, plus a little Python I run on my laptop. **There is no backend.** Both halves are
ports-and-adapters with a pure domain at the centre:

```
web/  PWA, zero runtime deps             api/  Python tooling, not a server
  domain   timing, prompt, model pick      domain     features, Naismith baseline
  ports    LanguageModel, Predictor        adapters   TabPFN, hikes CSV, fort trails
  app      planTrek, askFort, offline      evaluation leave-one-out vs Naismith
  adapters WebLLM (Gemma), table, data     precompute → web/public/predictions.json
```

95 web tests and 23 Python tests. CI runs both on every push, including the real TabPFN model.

## How I Built It

### Gemma, on the phone

The Ask screen runs Gemma through [WebLLM](https://github.com/mlc-ai/web-llm), which compiles
models to WebGPU. WebLLM is imported from a CDN at runtime, so the web app has **no runtime
dependencies**: TypeScript compiles straight to ES modules and there's no bundler.

Which Gemma? That depends on the phone, so the choice is a small pure function. It takes the newest
supported generation that fits under ~2.6B parameters, uses q4f16 if the GPU supports `shader-f16`
(half the memory of q4f32), and avoids WebLLM's `-1k` builds, because the fort notes plus the
question don't fit in 1,024 tokens. I tested the picker against the real model list WebLLM ships,
not a hand-written one.

My first pick was **Gemma 3 1B**: the newest and smallest, a 600 MB download. It loaded, and then
answered "What happened here in history?" with "- Sinhagad" fifty times. Gemma 3 mixes 512-token
local-attention layers with global ones, and WebLLM 0.2 can give the whole model only one attention
window. Switch it off and the local layers read the full ~2,000-token fort prompt they were never
trained on. Switch it on and every layer forgets the fort notes after 512 tokens. So Killedar runs
**Gemma 2 2B (q4f16, about 1.5 GB, downloaded once)**, whose local window equals its context. It's a
bigger download, but its answers come from the notes.

Small models make things up, so the prompt is built to keep the answers short and true:

- The fort data is rendered as **compact prose notes**, not JSON. Small models follow prose better,
  and it saves context.
- The instruction says *answer only from the notes; if they don't cover it, say so*, and **never
  invent bus times, distances or phone numbers**. On a mountain, a confident wrong answer is worse
  than "I don't know".
- Answers are capped at about 80 words, because the reader is walking.
- Gemma's chat template has no system role, so instruction, notes and question go in one user turn.

### TabPFN: a model of *me*, from a few dozen rows

Naismith's rule (an hour per 5 km plus an hour per 600 m of climb) is the classic estimate, and it
was written for Scottish hills, not for a laterite staircase at 9 a.m. in October humidity. The useful
question isn't "how long does Rajgad take" but "how long does Rajgad take **me**".

That's a regression problem with almost no data: my own hike history, a few dozen rows at best.
It's exactly the case [TabPFN](https://github.com/PriorLabs/TabPFN) is made for. TabPFN is a
pre-trained tabular foundation model, so "fitting" it on 25 rows is in-context learning. There's no
training loop and nothing to overfit with hyperparameters.

Features: distance, elevation gain, start hour, group size. Target: trailhead-to-summit minutes.
The evaluation is leave-one-out, so each hike is predicted by a model that never saw it:

<!-- TODO: put your real hikes in api/data/hikes.csv, then run

     and paste the numbers below.

     Naismith 35.9 min). If you submit before replacing it, you must say so: replace the table with
     "These numbers are from a synthetic placeholder dataset; my real hikes go in next." -->
| | Mean absolute error (leave-one-out, N hikes) |
|---|---|
| Naismith's rule | **XX min** |
| TabPFN on my hikes | **XX min** |

<!-- TODO: one honest sentence interpreting it, e.g. "Naismith thinks I'm faster than I am on steep
ground; TabPFN noticed." If TabPFN didn't win, say so; that's a result too. -->

My first version served TabPFN from a small web API on Render. It worked, but it was the wrong shape
twice over. It needed signal, which is the one thing this app can't assume. And PyTorch plus TabPFN
sat right at the 512 MB limit of a free instance, so every prediction knocked the server over.

The fix was to notice how small the question space is. The app only ever asks about its own trails,
at a start hour between 4 and 14 and a group of 1 to 30. That's about 1,650 questions. So TabPFN
answers **all of them ahead of time**, on my laptop, in about 13 seconds:

```bash
python -m killedar_api.precompute data/hikes.csv   # → web/public/predictions.json (7 KB)
```

The app ships that file and the service worker caches it. The Plan screen looks up *my* climb time
in about 20 ms, online or on the summit, and anything outside the table falls back to Naismith.
TabPFN still does the learning; the phone just reads its answers.

### Narration with ElevenLabs

The Listen screen plays each fort's history in English and in Marathi, narrated by ElevenLabs.
The narration is generated **once, at build time**, by
[`web/scripts/generate-audio.ts`](https://github.com/abhijeetkaze/killedar/blob/main/web/scripts/generate-audio.ts):
it sends each history to the ElevenLabs text-to-speech API and writes the MP3s into
`web/public/audio/`. Six clips, 1.4 MB in all, committed with the app and saved for offline with
everything else. On the fort they play with no signal and no API key, and listening costs nothing.

Marathi was the catch. The usual `eleven_multilingual_v2` model rejects it outright
(`does not support language_code 'mr'`), so the script uses **`eleven_v3`** and sends each clip's
language code, which means the Marathi history is read as Marathi. If a fort has no clip yet, the app
falls back to the phone's own speech synthesis.

### Offline setup

"Works offline" is something you should be able to see. A **Use offline** button in the header opens
a short checklist: the app files first (about 2 MB: shell, fort notes, climb-time table, narration),
then the Gemma model (about 1.5 GB). Each step has its own progress bar, the button becomes a
progress ring, and it turns into a green **Offline ready** check when everything is on the phone.
If the phone runs out of storage, it says so plainly instead of failing quietly. If the browser has
no WebGPU, Plan and Listen still go offline and the checklist says why Ask can't.

### Facts about real places

Fort data is facts about real mountains, and wrong facts there have consequences. Every fort file
cites its sources and stays `"verified": false` until it's been checked. Bus times are **left blank
on purpose**: the app asks you for the last bus rather than guessing one, because rural ST timings
change and a hallucinated 6:30 p.m. bus is how people end up walking down in the dark.

### Deploy

One [`render.yaml`](https://github.com/abhijeetkaze/killedar/blob/main/render.yaml) blueprint deploys
the PWA to Render as a static site: the app, the fort notes, the TabPFN table and the narration. That's
the whole deployment. Gemma runs on the phone, so there is no server to keep awake or pay for.

## Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

Because the top of a Sahyadri fort has no signal, and that settles the argument.

A closed model behind an API is a service. It's there when the network is, when the bill is paid,
and when the provider still offers it. On Rajgad's Balekilla none of those hold. Open weights are
an **artifact**: once they're on the phone, nobody can switch them off, rate-limit them or price them
per question.

That's also why the one closed service in Killedar, ElevenLabs, runs only at build time. Its output
is an MP3 that ships with the app, so nothing on the mountain depends on it.

Running on the device also keeps things private. My hike history (where I go, when, how slowly)
goes into TabPFN on my own laptop, and only the predicted minutes ship with the app. Questions asked
on the fort never leave the phone at all.

It also matters who gets to build. Everything in Killedar is open: Gemma's weights, WebLLM's
compiler, TabPFN's model, the fort notes and their sources. So a trekking group in Nashik can fork
it, add Harishchandragad, correct my Marathi, and ship their own version without asking anyone's
permission or paying for anyone's API. Forts were built to stand on their own when cut off. The tool
for climbing them should too.

## Prize Categories

- **Best Use of Gemma.** Gemma 2 2B runs entirely on the phone through WebLLM and answers questions
  about each fort in English or Marathi, offline, grounded only in that fort's cited notes. A tested
  pure function picks the build that fits the device. See `web/src/adapters/webllmModel.ts`,
  `web/src/domain/model.ts` and `web/src/domain/prompt.ts`.
- **Best Use of TabPFN.** TabPFN learns my personal climb time from my hike history (a CSV),
  evaluated leave-one-out against Naismith's rule. Its predictions for every trail, start hour and
  group size are precomputed into the app, so Plan uses them offline on the fort. See
  `api/killedar_api/precompute.py` and `api/killedar_api/evaluation.py`; CI runs both with the real
  model.
- **Best Use of ElevenLabs.** Fort histories are narrated with the ElevenLabs API (`eleven_v3`, with
  per-clip language codes so Marathi works) at build time. Six clips ship with the app and play on
  the summit with no signal. See `web/scripts/generate-audio.ts` and `web/public/audio/`.
- **Best Use of Render.** Render hosts the app's front end: the whole PWA, deployed as a static site
  from one `render.yaml` blueprint, with the TabPFN table and narration served alongside it.

---

I re-read the contest page and updated [docs/dev-post.md](docs/dev-post.md) to match it. It's committed locally but not pushed.

**Template fixes:**
- **Opening line** now matches the official wording: *"This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 1: Touch Grass"*.
- **What I Built** now answers the template's two questions directly. *Who it's for*: the weekend crowd leaving Pune before dawn who lose signal on the way up. *How it gets you off the screen*: one time to remember, short answers, and history read aloud while you look at the walls.
- **Why Open Innovation** now opens with the template's question, *"what did it make possible that a closed API wouldn't?"*: with a closed API, Ask would be a spinner on the summit.
- **My Agent Session** (optional, DevRelay) is added as a hidden placeholder. The page says judges find it helpful.
- **Stale facts are fixed:** "95 web tests", "Use offline", and all three screens now work offline. A new "Offline setup" section covers the opt-in flow.

**Prize categories:** only the four that apply, each saying what's used and where to look in the code:

| Category | Page wording | How Killedar uses it |
|---|---|---|
| Gemma | "run it locally" | Gemma 2 2B on the phone via WebLLM, answering offline from cited notes |
| TabPFN | "predict … from historical data like a CSV" | Personal climb-time model from a hikes CSV, precomputed so it works offline |
| ElevenLabs | "…generate narration for your demo" | `eleven_v3` narration in English and Marathi, made at build time and played offline |
| Render | "host an agent's front end" | Hosts the whole PWA from one `render.yaml` |

The post now also says honestly that ElevenLabs is the one closed service and runs only at build time. I left out Tinker, Arduino and Backboard because the project doesn't use them.
